title: The Fed traces how an investment setback could reach lenders through leases, collateral and funding
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: An investment disappointment becomes a financial-stability problem when the people who must absorb losses also have to raise cash or cut credit. The Board’s November report finds several places where that could happen, particularly in the financing of advanced computing and among leveraged investors. It also identifies substantial cushions. Banks reported high regulatory capital, most homeowners held considerable equity, and investment-grade companies generally had strong interest coverage. The report was published on 13 November and generally incorporates information through 28 October. Its estimates refer to different observation periods. The latest comprehensive hedge-fund filings, for example, cover the first quarter, well before the October market observations.

Expensive assets leave less room for disappointing cash flows. Section 1 finds that higher expected earnings reduced the forward equity price-to-earnings ratio over the past year, yet its level remained well above its historical median. The gap between the forward earnings yield and the real ten-year Treasury yield was near the low end of its own range. These are valuation indicators, each dependent on earnings expectations. They do not supply a probability or date for a correction. Two- and ten-year Treasury yields rose markedly from the preceding report, and an estimated term premium rose above its median. The appendix identifies the premium as a model estimate using the yield curve and interest-rate forecasts. Treating the entire change in a Treasury yield as a revision to the expected policy rate would conflate two different sources of repricing.

Market liquidity had a less uniform reading. The price response to a given order imbalance was near its post-2014 median for the liquid ten-year note and appreciably above its median for the two-year note. Even so, the recent increase in price impact was small relative to the rise in volatility. Corporate bond bid-ask spreads remained tight in the third quarter. That combination describes trading conditions observed to date. A question for stress analysis is how much collateral could be sold or financed if multiple funds needed to reduce risk simultaneously. Depth in a normal trading session gives only part of the answer.

Aggregate debt growth also concealed substantial differences between borrowers. Table 2.1 places US nonfinancial business and household credit at $45.3 trillion in the second quarter, up 4.6% over twelve months against nominal GDP growth of 6.6%. A falling ratio can therefore coexist with rising debt in dollars. Investment-grade firms accounted for more than three-quarters of the debt of publicly traded nonfinancial firms and had strong interest coverage. Some private and lower-rated public borrowers had weaker capacity to service debt, particularly where borrowing rates reset quickly or maturities were short. The private-credit default rate rose toward the top of its short historical range even as some measures of loans ceasing to accrue interest eased slightly. Payment of interest by adding it to principal can postpone the cash test.

Housing offers another distinction between a valuation warning and a credit warning. Prices remained high relative to rents. Yet mortgage balances relative to property values were well below earlier peaks, negative equity was rare, and delinquencies on conventional mortgages were near historical lows. Delinquencies on FHA mortgages continued to rise. Commercial property had a different risk. Stable transaction prices and rents could coexist with a refinancing problem when a large loan matures. Lenders’ willingness to extend or restructure maturing loans had limited forced sales. The report also warns that late-2026 maturities in non-agency commercial mortgage-backed securities represent only part of the overall commercial property debt market. Extrapolating those loans’ refinancing pressure to every building would misstate the scale.

Box 2.2 maps the fastest-changing credit exposure. Tracked advanced-computing debt issuance exceeded $680 billion by October 2026, compared with $130 billion during all of 2023. Outstanding public debt connected to the buildout exceeded $1.1 trillion. The first number is issuance over a period, the second a stock on a date, and some privately placed deals are outside the issuance data. Five large cloud companies’ strong cash flows initially let them fund considerable investment internally, a material difference from the telecom investment comparison in Figure B. More debt issuance and a greater reliance on project finance now make contractual risk allocation increasingly important.

A developer can use a long lease from a highly rated customer to borrow for construction. A chip supplier can guarantee a minimum future value for hardware pledged as collateral. Both arrangements help finance firms with weaker standalone credit. They also return part of the risk to the stronger counterparty if usage, rents or equipment values disappoint. For the seven technology firms in Figure C, undiscounted leases awaiting commencement exceeded $1 trillion. Other potential or contracted obligations, including minimum payments and residual-value guarantees, exceeded $2 trillion. Footnote 5 explains why adding these amounts to the carrying value of debt would produce a misleading total. The payment schedules, triggers and valuation bases differ. Senior lenders, subordinated investors and guarantors would also absorb losses at different stages. A strong counterparty can absorb a loss that would otherwise reach lenders, subject to its own ability to honour the contract.

The report’s new Financial Accounts categories help locate the intermediaries. Box 2.1 says domestic and foreign private-credit vehicles held about $1.5 trillion in loans to US businesses at the end of 2025. The new accounting also moved some liabilities previously reported elsewhere into measured nonfinancial business debt. A rise in a newly integrated series should be checked against classification changes before it is read as new borrowing. Bank commitments to other financial institutions exceeded $2.8 trillion in 2026 Q2. Roughly a quarter belonged to the combined private-equity, business-development-company and private-credit category. Commitments indicate the possibility of later funding needs. They are a different measure from drawn balances or credit losses.

Two channels could amplify a price correction. First, hedge-fund filings for the first quarter put gross notional exposure relative to net asset value at its highest since the comprehensive series began in 2013. Leverage was concentrated among larger funds and supported equity, interest-rate and Treasury strategies even as basis-trade activity declined. Later dealer surveys indicated little change in clients’ leverage in the second and third quarters. The filings measure a level and the survey measures reported changes over a subsequent interval. Gross notional exposure includes derivatives and is distinct from the ratio of balance-sheet assets to net asset value. Second, a fall in the value of fixed-rate securities can make the means of raising liquidity matter for banks. The fair value of their available-for-sale and held-to-maturity portfolios was roughly $330 billion below combined book value in Q2. Selling a held-to-maturity asset can crystallize a loss. Pledging it for repo funding can raise cash while leaving the security on the books, provided that funding remains available.

Funding risks were moderate in the Board’s aggregate assessment. Table 4.1 nevertheless identifies about $28.2 trillion of money-like liabilities potentially subject to withdrawal or rollover, equivalent to 87% of GDP in Q2. Government money funds accounted for most of the increase in cash-management assets and historically faced fewer large redemptions than institutional prime funds. Requests to redeem from certain nontraded private-credit vehicles eased through Q3 but remained elevated. Quarterly redemption limits helped those vehicles manage the timing of payments while net flows remained negative. The experience of meeting redemption requests subject to a limit does not establish what the underlying loans could fetch in an immediate sale.

Box 5.1 reports a different kind of evidence. Of 23 market contacts consulted during September and October, 87% cited AI-related risks over the next 12–18 months, including a reversal of valuations, complex financing or operational disruption. The spring exercise had 20 respondents. These percentages measure the salience of a concern among contacts. They are neither default probabilities nor the Board’s forecast. The separate scenario discussion shows how a disappointment in returns on investment, a disruption to a common service provider or higher energy prices and long rates might interact with existing vulnerabilities. None of these scenarios constitutes an FOMC decision, and none measures a market reaction to publication of this report.

questions.question: Who would need cash first if data-centre occupancy or equipment resale values fell?
questions.detail: Map a representative project from its senior and subordinated financing through the developer, anchor tenant and equipment guarantor. Separate mandatory lease payments from contingent guarantees and record both their triggers and due dates. Compare the stressed cash flows with liquid resources at each entity. The undiscounted gross commitments in Box 2.2 can locate exposures but cannot be entered as a single immediate loss.

questions.question: Would a Treasury sell-off produce fund deleveraging, a bank capital loss, or both?
questions.detail: For funds, align changes in financing haircuts, margin requirements and positions by strategy. For banks, distinguish securities sold at a loss from pledged holdings and monitor dependence on rolling repo. Compare these indicators with price impact at two and ten years. Use the dates of the underlying fund filings and securities data, since the November publication does not make each observation current in October.

questions.question: Is deteriorating credit quality concentrated among borrowers whose payments reset soon?
questions.detail: Separate floating-rate and near-maturity borrowers from investment-grade issuers with fixed debt. Within the weaker group, compare cash interest coverage, interest added to principal, distressed exchanges and cash defaults. Check whether the new Financial Accounts classification changes the denominator. Distinguish new extensions from use of existing lines before inferring a contraction in the supply of credit.

questions.question: Which vehicles could meet withdrawals only by transferring liquidity pressure elsewhere?
questions.detail: Track redemption requests, limits, realised sales and new inflows separately for nontraded private-credit funds. Compare these with outflows from daily-dealing bond funds and the availability of bank credit lines. A fall in paid redemptions is less reassuring when unfulfilled requests rise. The contact survey can guide scenario selection, but loss estimates require portfolio quantities, funding terms and transaction prices.
